hook: You know “Don’t judge”. But did you know the same paragraph ends with helping your brother get the speck out of his eye?
known: Many people know this verse as a call not to look down on others.
who: Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5 to 7).
audience: His disciples, with the crowds listening (Matthew 5:1-2).
setting: Part of a long teaching on how his followers are to live with God and with one another.
around: The next verses give the reason and a picture: “with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you”, and a man with a beam in his own eye offering to remove a speck from his brother’s. Jesus does not end by leaving the speck where it is. He ends: “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.”
point: The warning is against hypocritical judgment, the kind that sees faults in others and not in oneself. The passage still expects followers of Jesus to help one another see clearly, after looking at themselves first.
story:
He held no office and had no famous teacher behind him. In his home town they asked, “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?” He went up a hillside, sat down and began to speak, and the world has not finished listening.

He did not lean on the great names. He spoke as if the last word was his to give. Love your enemies. Pray for those who mistreat you. Take the beam out of your own eye first. When he stopped, Matthew says, “the multitudes were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes.”

Some of it had been said before. Israel’s Scriptures already told God’s people to love their neighbor and to feed an enemy who is hungry (Leviticus 19:18, Proverbs 25:21). What Jesus does is gather it, sharpen it and ask for all of it, from the heart, toward everyone.

The astonishment never quite wore off. Centuries later, people far outside the church were still stopped by this sermon, as the voices below show.
